book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook opens with the definition (a mutual fund pools money from many investors and invests it in securities), then lists types and NAV. Here the learner is first placed in the investor's chair with four problems, the fix (pool money, hire a professional) is built as a picture, and only then is it named 'mutual fund'. NAV comes next with one worked number example, units and growth follow from it, and only after that the two structural types are shown on one timeline, with open-ended taught as the close-ended picture minus its rules. The company (AMC) and the regulator's categories come last, as context.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Start from the person's problem, build the solution, name it; then cut the solution by its moving parts (price of a unit, entry and exit over time, who runs it, what it holds), each on the same running picture.

narration.density: About 20 terms (portfolio, diversification, collective fund, professional management, asset class, ticket size, mutual fund, NAV, total assets, liabilities, units, open-ended, close-ended, launch date, maturity date, NFO, NFO period, AMC, SEBI, equity/debt/hybrid/solution-oriented funds, index fund, ETF, fund of funds) in about 540 s, about 2.3 per minute. talmel_summary: Picture and voice land together on most tiles (within about 1 s); when one leads it is by 1.5-3 s. The fit is strongest where the step itself is drawn: notes flowing into the cart on 'ikattha', each NAV number landing on its own bar, and the open-ended fund made by dissolving the exchange panel as the voice says 'not traded'. Many other changes only write the spoken word as a label (challenges, high risk, number of units), and several spoken facts get no picture at all: Rs 1000 -> 100 units, buying at the current NAV, the maturity payout, SEBI, and the index-fund idea. One transcript gap (about 456-469 s) has no tile in it.

voice.notes: Fast and even, about 190 recognised words per minute, little pausing. Talks to the learner as 'hum log' and 'aap', so the opening reads as the viewer's own problem. Signposts are frequent and clear ('chaliye ab baat karte hain', 'sabse pehle', 'ab dekhte hain'). Numbers read in Indian units (1 crore, 10 lakh, 9 lakh, 10 rupees) and each spoken once, slowly enough to follow. Uses 'lekin/bat', 'yaani', 'jabki' as hinges. Ends quickly; the category part is read at the same speed as a list, with no stress on the key words.

game_ideas.player_does: Is one of six small investors with Rs 1000 each; first tries to buy a large-ticket bond (Rs 5000) and a spread of shares alone, then drops the money into the shared fund cart and picks a manager.
game_ideas.process_happens: Alone, the bond is locked ('ticket too big') and the one share bought swings wildly; in the cart the six notes become one pot, the manager splits it into equity, debt and gold, and a risk meter calms.
game_ideas.win: Reach a diversified pot whose risk meter stays in the green.
game_ideas.lose: Keeping the money alone shows the high-risk game: one bad share wipes out the whole stake.
game_ideas.concept: pooling into a collective fund run by a professional manager = mutual fund

game_ideas.player_does: Runs the fund's NAV board: moves sliders for asset value, running costs and units, and sells units to arriving investors.
game_ideas.process_happens: NAV recomputes live as (assets - liabilities) / units; each investor's rupees turn into units at the current NAV, and when markets rise the green arrows climb from assets to NAV to each investor's holding.
game_ideas.win: Price every sale at the current NAV so that old investors' unit value is unchanged by new entries.
game_ideas.lose: Selling units at an old NAV shows existing investors' value dropping (dilution), explaining why everyone must buy at the current NAV.
game_ideas.concept: units: investment = units x NAV; buying at current NAV

game_ideas.player_does: Given a fund's timeline, a learner who wants to enter or exit at different days (during NFO, mid-life, after maturity) chooses the door: buy from the fund, buy on the stock exchange, or redeem.
game_ideas.process_happens: For a close-ended fund the fund's door shuts after the NFO band and only the exchange door works until maturity; switching the fund to open-ended removes the exchange door and the maturity end, and the units counter starts moving.
game_ideas.win: Every entry and exit goes through the right door for the fund type and day.
game_ideas.lose: Trying to buy new units from a close-ended fund mid-life shows the shut window and the 'units are fixed' counter.
game_ideas.concept: close-ended funds: NFO window, fixed units traded on the stock market, maturity

game_ideas.player_does: Sorts fund cards by what they hold or aim for (only shares; corporate and government bonds; both; retirement or child's education; tracks Nifty) into SEBI's five bins, then picks one for an investor profile (age, goal, risk appetite).
game_ideas.process_happens: Each card opens to show its basket of assets; the investor's goal meter and risk meter react to the pick.
game_ideas.win: All cards in the right bins and a fund matched to the investor's goal and risk.
game_ideas.lose: A cautious retiree put into an equity fund shows the risk meter in red.
game_ideas.concept: SEBI's five categories of mutual funds

notes_questions.q: Ek chhote investor ke liye akele stock market mein invest karne mein kaun-si chaar mushkilein hain?
Mutual fund in mushkilon ko kaise solve karta hai? Paisa investor se asset class tak kaise jata hai?
NAV kaise nikalte hain? Assets 1 crore, liabilities 10 lakh, units 9 lakh ho to NAV kitna?
NAV badhne par investor ka paisa kyon badhta hai, aur naya investor kis NAV par units khareedta hai?
Close-ended fund ki life mein NFO period, maturity tak ka samay, aur maturity ke baad kya hota hai?
Open-ended aur close-ended funds mein units, entry-exit, stock market aur maturity ka farq kya hai?

SEBI ke anusaar mutual funds ki paanch categories kaun-si hain, aur har ek kahan paisa lagati hai?

checks_learned: Every spoken worked number (Rs 1000 -> 100 units) must appear on screen at its moment; a spoken example with no visual is flagged.
A value written on screen more than 3 s before it is spoken (10 lakh liabilities) should be timed to its spoken word.
An on-screen sentence with a double negative ('no new units ... is not issued') must be caught by a text check before render.
When the script names a regulator or rule-maker (SEBI), the scene must show who made the rule, not only the list.
A list of more than three categories must give each item a picture of what it holds; a text list on screen for over 30 s without a new visual is flagged.

Absolute claims ('open-ended units never trade on the stock market', 'retail investors cannot buy government bonds') must be checked against known exceptions (ETFs, retail G-sec access) before they reach the script.

A comparison of two types that share a structure should reuse the first picture and strike or remove what differs (done well here: the close-ended timeline becomes open-ended); enforce reuse over a fresh second drawing.
Spoken rules with no change on screen for more than 15 s (maturity payout, buying at current NAV) need a matching visual step.

teaching_best.why: The learner is placed in the investor's chair with four concrete problems, so the mutual fund arrives as the answer to a felt need before it is named.
'Kya ho agar hum sab paisa ikattha karein': the solution is built as a what-if, and each challenge is answered in turn (expertise, time, ticket size, diversification).
One worked example with round Indian numbers (1 crore, 10 lakh, 9 lakh) gives NAV = Rs 10, then carries on into units and growth.
Open-ended is taught as the close-ended fund minus its rules, with 'jabki' recalling the fixed units, so the difference is the lesson.

teaching_weak.why: The rule 'buy at current NAV' is stated as obvious ('aap samajh rahe honge') without the reason (fairness to existing investors) or a number.
Maturity payout and 'may become open-ended' are said quickly with no example.
Five SEBI categories and three 'other' kinds in under two minutes as a list; solution-oriented schemes partly lost in a transcript gap; ETFs pushed to another video.
Doubtful as stated: retail investors can buy government bonds in India today (retail G-sec access); describe, do not certify.
Doubtful as stated: 'open-ended units do not trade on the stock market' clashes with ETFs, which the same video lists later.
